chunks: How many targets fit on an I2C bus. The question: How many slaves can there be?
There are two limits on how many chips an I2C bus can hold. The address limit: a 7-bit address gives 128 codes, but 16 are reserved, so 112 chips at most.
The electrical limit is tighter.
Every chip pin and centimeter of wiring adds a little capacitance (stored charge), and the pull-up resistor must fill all of it each time a wire rises.
Too much makes the rise too slow, and that usually stops you first.
Picture a bridge with 112 numbered parking spots and a weight limit. Each parked car adds weight, and so does every meter of road.
You hit the weight limit long before the last spot fills. The spots are the addresses, and the weight is the capacitance.
The 7-bit space has 128 codes. The lowest 8 (0x00 to 0x07) and the highest 8 (0x78 to 0x7 farads) are reserved for special functions, leaving the green 112 for ordinary targets.
In 10-bit addressing the 0x78 to 0x7B block is the prefix that announces a two-byte address.
Usable addresses: the 112 of the 128 possible 7-bit codes that ordinary chips may use.
Bus capacitance: the total load on a wire from pins, traces and connectors, in picofarads (pF). The spec caps it at 400 picofarads ("What is I2C bus capacitance").
Pull-up resistor: the resistor that lifts a wire to high, whose value is limited on both sides ("I2C pull-ups: why and how to size").
Rise time: how long a wire takes to climb from low to high. It must stay under 300 nanoseconds at 400 kilohertz.
Multiplexer: a chip that connects one of several side-branches to the main bus, so each branch carries only its own load.
Suppose each chip pin adds 10 picofarads, and traces and connectors add 60 picofarads. At the 400 picofarads limit, that is (400-60) over 10 equals 34 chips.
With a 25% margin, 300 picofarads, it is (300-60) over 10 equals 24 chips. At 400 kilohertz and 3.
3 volts, no pull-up value works above about 366 picofarads: one strong enough to rise in time draws more current than the chips can pull low.
So 300 picofarads is the sensible limit. Shared default addresses can limit you sooner. That is the whole idea.
"Addressing-wise, 7 bits give 128 codes, 16 reserved, so 112 targets; 10-bit addressing gives about a thousand.
But the real limit is electrical: total bus capacitance is capped at 400 picofarads, and each device and each centimetre of trace adds capacitance, which slows the rise time.
In practice that's around 20 to 40 devices. Beyond that, or when addresses collide, you use address pins, an I2C multiplexer or a bus buffer."
